book: How Search Decides What You See
author: Aaron Tay

episodes.title: Save the search, not just the question
episodes.subtitle: Reproducibility, transformations, and recorded runs

scenes.title: The search box has a backstage
scenes.claim: Libraries need to record, inspect, test, and require
scenes.narration: Welcome to our cosmic library. A friendly search box offers an answer. Behind it, machines transform the question, retrieve candidates, combine lists, and change the order. Chapter fifteen turns the book's technical distinctions into professional practice. Before trusting the performance, we need a record of what happened backstage.

scenes.title: Same question. A moving system.
scenes.claim: Reproducibility is conditional on records, versions, and configuration
scenes.narration: Type the same question tomorrow and the results may change. Coverage, indexing, vocabulary, models, and ranking settings can move. Boolean eligibility is repeatable under fixed conditions. New records can change B M twenty-five's collection statistics. Dense retrieval is not inherently random either. No method guarantees the same live results forever.

scenes.title: Four compartments in the flight recorder
scenes.claim: Interpretation • candidates • ranking and fusion • retrieval control
scenes.narration: Pack the search record into four compartments. Query interpretation stores the input, transformations, and filters. Candidate retrieval stores the collection, fields, indexed units, method, and cut-offs. Ranking and fusion store how lists were combined and ordered. Retrieval control stores the arrangement and the path actually taken. One saved question cannot describe all four.

scenes.title: What was actually sent onward?
scenes.claim: Save exact transformed inputs; record whether reruns reuse or regenerate them
scenes.narration: Our search robot receives a question and writes a different retrieval input. Save that exact generated query, expansion, subquery, or hypothetical text, together with extracted filters. Record the prompt and model version where exposed. On a rerun, did the system reuse this saved transformation, or generate a new one? Those are different comparisons.

scenes.title: The route belongs in the record
scenes.claim: Fixed rules, adaptive branches, and agentic trajectories need different records
scenes.narration: A fixed pipeline follows a planned sequence. An adaptive pipeline chooses among branches the designer specified; record the branch and its selection rule. An agentic controller can plan its next action from returned observations. Record every query, selected source, route, observation, budget, and stopping point. Save the action and observation trace of the actual run.

scenes.title: A model name is only one setting
scenes.claim: Indexed units, analysis, similarity, search procedure, and cut-offs also matter
scenes.narration: The settings live in different places. Lexical retrieval needs compatible analysis and scoring configuration. Dense retrieval needs the encoder, embedded text, chunking, stored vectors, similarity function, and exact or approximate search settings. Sparse expansions and token alignments add their own inspectable layers. Ask for the configuration actually used, including candidate boundaries.

scenes.title: Start with the record you can make today
scenes.claim: Keep observed evidence, vendor documentation, and unknowns separate
scenes.narration: You can start today: save the input, product and mode, date, visible transformation, filters, reported count, result identifiers, and observed limitations. Export the raw results where possible. Mark each fact as observed, vendor documented, or unknown. Some versions and budgets require disclosure. An empty field is more honest than an invented setting.

scenes.title: A saved run is a baseline
scenes.claim: A recorded search supports comparison even when exact recreation is unavailable
scenes.narration: Exact future recreation may be unavailable, but the saved run still lets us compare. Which records disappeared? Which ranks changed? Which transformation changed? Preserve the exact inputs, identifiers, exports, and versions available at the time. Recording does not freeze the universe. It gives a later search something concrete to be compared against.

episodes.title: Follow the evidence behind a result
episodes.subtitle: Interpretability and faithful execution traces

scenes.title: Three qualities. Three questions.
scenes.claim: Transparency, interpretability, and understandability overlap but differ
scenes.narration: A vendor opens a curtain. That is transparency: information is exposed. We trace why a record was admitted, scored, or reranked. That is interpretability. We form an accurate, usable mental model. That is understandability. These overlap, but a broad product description or an overwhelming score display does not automatically provide all three.

scenes.title: A convincing story is not a trace
scenes.claim: Figure 15.1 is hypothetical; a generated rationale alone proves no executed stage
scenes.narration: Meet paper P in the chapter's hypothetical example. It appears at rank three. A generated explanation says it closely addresses our question about open access and citations. That sounds helpful. It does not establish which operation admitted P, or which stage put it third. A plausible description of relevance is not recorded search evidence.

scenes.title: Connect the question to the executed query
scenes.claim: Mock trace: lexical retrieval over abstracts matched open access and citations
scenes.narration: Now inspect the mock trace. The original question asks whether open access increases citations. The transformed query is open access as a phrase, AND a citation stem. The selected route is lexical retrieval over indexed abstracts. P's abstract contains open access and citations. This connects the record to stated operations, assuming those facts came from the executed search.

scenes.title: Candidate 18 becomes displayed result 3
scenes.claim: Mock trace: 18 of 100 candidates → reranked to 3 → displayed inside top 10
scenes.narration: In the chapter's mock trace, P was candidate eighteen among one hundred supplied records. A reranker moved it to rank three, inside the first ten displayed results. We can now locate the stages responsible for admission and position. The reranker's internal scoring details remain undisclosed. That gap stays visible; a fluent narrative must not fill it as fact.

scenes.title: Walk backwards from the result
scenes.claim: Inspection order reverses the search path; it is not execution order
scenes.narration: Figure fifteen point two walks the trail backwards. Start with the displayed record. Check fusion and display, scoring and reranking, matched evidence, candidate source, transformed query, and original query. This is inspection order, not execution order. Every step asks a different question. Where the evidence stops tells us what the product still leaves unexplained.

scenes.title: Each window shows one layer
scenes.claim: Visible terms, similarities, and alignments have limits on what they establish
scenes.narration: A Boolean clause explains eligibility, not relevance. A lexical score shows contributions, not a probability of relevance. Dense similarity identifies an indexed unit and comparison, but does not give a simple reason for every latent feature. Sparse terms and token alignments expose a layer. Highlights and attractive snippets do not, by themselves, explain final position.

scenes.title: Actions and observations leave footprints
scenes.claim: An agent's narrated reasoning is not evidence of what drove its choices
scenes.narration: For an agentic search, ask what tool was called, what query was sent, what came back, and what happened next. Keep the sequence and stopping decision. The model may also tell a story about its reasoning. That account can help orientation, but it is not evidence of what caused the choices. Label interpretation separately from the recorded trace.

scenes.title: Enough visibility to act
scenes.claim: A rerunnable search may still be opaque; an explanation may still be unrecorded
scenes.narration: We do not need every model weight to diagnose an unexpected result. We need an accurate mental model and an actionable trail, with unknowns clearly marked. A documented search can still be poorly understood. A clear explanation can still lack the inputs and outputs needed for comparison. Ask separately what can be saved, and what can be traced.

episodes.title: Questions to ask before you buy
episodes.subtitle: Nineteen questions across six evaluation groups

scenes.title: What starts a search, and who steers it?
scenes.claim: Group 1 • Questions 1–2: interpretation, transformations, and control
scenes.narration: Before comparing query boxes, ask what can start a search: text, controlled fields, a seed record, citation links, saved judgements, or API predicates. Group one asks what the system infers, changes, and decides, and who controls the trajectory. Can users inspect and export every transformed input and route? For agentic modes, include the task brief, observations, and stopping point.

scenes.title: Open the architecture diagram
scenes.claim: Group 2 • Questions 3–7: components, model roles, units, chunks, and fusion
scenes.narration: Group two asks which components retrieve and rank, and whether they run in parallel or sequence. What job does each model perform? What is indexed: titles, abstracts, passages, or articles? How are multiple chunks from one paper assembled? Where are hybrid lists fused and reranked, and what cut-offs apply? Later full-text fetching is a separate question from first-stage indexing.

scenes.title: Try the searches that break the demo
scenes.claim: Group 3 • Questions 8–10: exact matching, analysis, and failure tests
scenes.narration: Group three asks whether exact lexical matching survives for identifiers, chemical strings, gene names, and quoted phrases. How are punctuation, case, and hyphens analysed, and are query and document analysis compatible? Test unfamiliar strings, near-duplicate names, contradictory claims, negation, and exclusions. A beautiful paraphrase demonstration does not test whether the system preserved an exact requirement.

scenes.title: What taught the model relevance?
scenes.claim: Group 3 • Question 11: training signals and adaptation to local tasks
scenes.narration: The fourth question in group three asks what trained the relevance model. Web queries, question-answer pairs, citation links, and scholarly judgements teach different behaviours. How was the model adapted to the disciplines and document types being searched? A model name cannot answer that. Ask for evidence that its learned behaviour fits the tasks your library actually supports.

scenes.title: Make the evidence exportable
scenes.claim: Group 4 • Questions 12–14: traces, reruns, versions, and change notices
scenes.narration: Group four asks whether users can inspect why a result appeared, document and rerun the search, and identify model, index, and ranking changes. Export the actual transformed inputs, filters, routes, cut-offs, versions, and identifiers. Ask whether reruns reuse a saved transformation. Require a distinction between execution traces and post-hoc explanations, together with change notices that make comparisons possible.

scenes.title: Limits and retirement change the search
scenes.claim: Group 5 • Questions 15–16: costs, budget behaviour, and export before retirement
scenes.narration: Group five asks what a search costs and what happens at a limit. Does the system refuse, truncate results, or quietly search less deeply? Can the library see per-query consumption and agentic budgets? Then ask what happens when a mode is retired. Require notice and a route to export saved searches, sets, and traces while they remain accessible.

scenes.title: Bring your library's difficult questions
scenes.claim: Group 6 • Questions 17–19: local queries, known failures, and update comparisons
scenes.narration: Group six asks whose queries measured performance, whether failure cases were included, and whether the library can compare behaviour across an update. Bring your disciplines, languages, document types, vocabulary, and known relevant records. Save a baseline and rerun it after changes. Inspect individual failures as well as averages. A vendor's successful demonstration is evidence about that demonstration.

scenes.title: Require the trail before you need it
scenes.claim: Visibility to inspect • documentation to compare • control to test locally
scenes.narration: The printable vendor questionnaire collects all nineteen questions, with spaces for answers, evidence, verification, and follow-up. Request visibility, documentation, and control before licensing and renewal. These are features to require in advance. Record what was searched, trace what can be explained, and test the system locally. The library needs evidence it can use, not access to every model weight.
